They've fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades. A new ecovillage can't copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

texts.153g-P9fP10r:
After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving the Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. Their new arrangement moved authority toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community. Those local governments can coordinate through regional collectives, but the coordinating levels are explicitly described as depending on the communities instead of sitting above them.

Most institutions get more and more layers and offices as they age. The Zapatistas did a review of theirs, and then pushed authority down. Did they put out a book on leadership and open a certification program? Nope. They just went and changed the system they were actually living in.
texts.153g-P13q: Now, the Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path. (That's the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money.) Do their communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and resistance? Yes. But they also sell products and trade, and they get outside support. What they do show is that a community can stop buying major necessities and public functions on the market, and govern them collectively instead. And outside help can make a community more capable, sure, but it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

texts.153g-P17g: Sociocracy has a very different origin story from the Zapatistas, but it has arrived at some similar forms: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. texts.153g-P16b3P17j:
In my research, I also tried to follow what happened after the Escuelita. I found alumni networks, people bringing practices home, and organizing later on. What I didn't find was a clear chain from an Escuelita student to a newly founded communal institution, with evidence of how its members and their kids actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already traveling internationally before the Escuelita, so a resemblance later on doesn't prove by itself that it came from the Escuelita. I'm borrowing a way of teaching and the ambition to replicate, and I'm not claiming the Zapatistas have already proved my whole model.

Then there's sociocracy, which comes from a very different history but ended up with some similar forms: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels. Does that prove there's a universal formula? No. But it does give builders another serious system to study, so they're not making up their governance in the middle of their first dispute.
